newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Norma, Cherie stand by their men before UK election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Norma, Cherie stand by their men before UK election.

text.p: John Major's wife, Norma, uses teabags more than once and likes to freeze her left-over cheese.
Cherie, wife of opposition leader Tony Blair, is a dab hand at quick family meals and loves knitting sweaters.

With an election less than nine months off, Britain's two main parties are using every gun in their armoury to convince voters they understand what makes the country tick, and Norma and Cherie are in the frontline in their aprons.

The ruling Conservatives are convinced "First Lady" Norma is a vote-winner with middle class women because of her classic family role -- a mother of two who stayed at home supporting her husband while John climbed to the top of the political ladder.

But Labour strategists think Cherie's home life is more relevant to modern Britain. They believe voters are impressed she can combine her busy life as a top lawyer with raising three children and keeping the home fires burning.
In the weeks before this year's annual party conferences, when newspaper columnists will report on every hair tint and smile, the battle of the wives has been joined in earnest.
Norma has given her first press interviews, six years after husband John first moved into 10, Downing Street.

"Domestic life suits me," says Norma, 54. Apart from squeezing the last drops out of tea bags, Norma has spent the last year working on a book on the prime minister's official country house, Chequers, which is published later this month.
Norma is so good around the house that John used to ring her for help when they were first dating. "All my lights have gone off. What do I do?" John asked once when a fuse blew.
Considered more politically radical than Tony, Cherie took a tentative step into the media world by editing this month's Prima, a cooking-and-hairstyles women's magazine.

"Sometimes I think I'm just juggling all the balls in the air and I'm amazed that they don't fall down at once," she said, lauding the efforts of working mothers and home carers. Prima readers were told Tony was very good at polishing shoes but could not be said to be "intimate" with the washing machine.
While their politics, education and work experience are totally different, Norma and Cherie have a lot in common.

Neither expected to be the wife of a party leader, both found press attention hard to deal with and both took a long while to adjust to the public spotlight. Their marriages and families are the rocks on which they have built their lives.
Major's elevation to the top job in November 1990 ended Margaret Thatcher's 11-year reign and Denis Thatcher's time in Downing Street.
"Everything was so new and there was nobody to give me any guidance -- it had been a long time since there had been a prime minister's wife," Norma said this month.

The press could not resist snide, snobbish attacks on her naivety and her husband's ordinary background. She got "hammered" for wearing the same blue suit two days running shortly after John Major became leader, she admits now.

"I mean you know that's terrible, isn't it, and of course the suit was perceived to be a disaster as well. Life is full of adjustments and I think if life is going to be tolerable you've got to try and find a way to adjust to what life throws at you."

Norma decided to slip into the background. She supported her husband at official and political functions but preferred to stay at home in Huntingdon, central England, rather than live with him during the week in London.
The Blairs live about 20 minutes' drive from Downing Street, but Cherie says the whole family will move house if Labour, as indicated strongly by opinion polls, win the next election.
"Wherever Tony goes, we are going too. The most important thing is to keep the family together," she told Prima. "We want to keep life as normal as possible."
That's what Norma said in 1990, and Cherie has had enough experience since her husband took charge of Labour in July 1994 to know that life will never be the same if Blair wins.
The daughter of a well-known actor who starred in the television comedy series Till Death Us Do Part, Cherie was used at an early age to the pressure of fame.

She once complained that she started as the daughter of someone and is now the wife of someone. The 41-year-old has given speeches at conferences discussing battered women but has resisted the temptation to give a formal interview.
This has not stopped the Conservative press sniffing around her past, trying to find evidence she is a closet left-winger at odds with her husband's push to the centre ground of politics.

They have had to content themselves with swipes at her dress sense -- a low point was when she turned up at a horse racing meet in pixie boots -- and her doting support for her husband in public, complete with fond gazes and an apparently rictus smile.
Despite the current publicity offensive and the interest of the media in their lives, both women appear determined to avoid becoming first ladies in the U.S. mould.

Cherie has been likened by Conservative newspapers to Hillary Clinton, said by some to be the power behind her husband's throne. But she says she intends to carry on working in law if Labour wins the election. She could become a judge during Tony's five-year term.
Norma shudders at the thought of being like Elizabeth Dole and addressing a party convention.
"I can't think of anything that would make me want to do that, however much I might love him. I don't think I'd want to take a microphone and make a public declaration of it."
